analysis.one_liner: Sets a single nationwide cap on smog-forming nitrogen oxide pollution from fossil-fuel power plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor and died in a House committee at the end of 1998.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any fossil-fuel power plant larger than 25 megawatts to emit more than 0.35 pounds of nitrogen oxides per million Btu, a uniform nationwide standard [S2][S3]. Nitrogen oxides are a main ingredient of ozone smog, and the bill's findings note that this pollution drifts across state lines and that patchwork rules can reward the dirtiest plants as electricity markets open to competition [S3]. Plants owned by the same company in one state could average their emissions instead of meeting the limit at every unit, and the EPA would write enforcement rules, with the standard taking effect for emissions after December 31, 2000 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downwind of coal- and gas-fired power plants, especially in states receiving pollution blown in from elsewhere. Tighter nitrogen oxide limits reduce ozone smog, which is linked to asthma attacks and other respiratory illness. The bill's own findings argue a uniform floor would stop competition in electricity markets from shifting generation toward plants with the weakest limits [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets one nationwide emission floor of 0.35 pounds of nitrogen oxides per million Btu for fossil-fuel utility units over 25 megawatts, replacing a patchwork of limits that vary by plant age, type, and location [S2][S3].

Treats the new limit as an enforceable emission limitation under the Clean Air Act, and bars any covered unit from operating after December 31, 2000 without a Clean Air Act permit, giving regulators and citizens court-enforceable tools [S2][S3].
Allows owners of multiple units in one state to meet the standard through averaged emissions across those units, giving utilities flexibility to cut the cheapest tons first [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of fossil-fuel power plants, primarily coal-fired utilities, which would need to install or upgrade nitrogen oxide controls or shift generation to cleaner units. Those compliance costs could be passed to electricity customers in utility rates [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs at older coal plants would be substantial, and utilities could pass at least part of them on to households and businesses through higher electric rates [S3].

A single nationwide rate ignores how much cheaper some reductions are than others; the within-state averaging option softens this but offers no help to a utility with only one plant, and it does not allow trading across state lines [S3].
Requiring EPA regulations within 60 days of enactment is an unusually tight deadline that could produce rushed rulemaking and litigation over the new standard [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefits of cutting smog-forming pollution from large power plants are broad and fall on the public, while the costs fall on a concentrated set of utilities and partly on their ratepayers. The bill is a fairly simple mandate with modest flexibility (state-level averaging), and it builds on existing Clean Air Act permitting rather than inventing a new system. Its main design weakness is the rigid uniform rate, which likely costs more per ton of pollution removed than a trading program would. Overall the benefits plausibly outweigh the costs, though an honest supporter should acknowledge the rate impact on customers of coal-heavy utilities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Commerce Committee, which sent it to two of its subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Julia Carson of Indiana introduced the bill on June 17, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce [S1][S5].
Nine days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it sat for the rest of the 105th Congress [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plant owners avoided the cost of new nationwide nitrogen oxide controls, while people living near and downwind of those plants kept breathing the existing levels of smog-forming pollution.

for.name: Rep. Julia Carson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Chair, House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, letting it die at the subcommittee referral stage.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so it never had visible support beyond its Democratic sponsor, and the Republican-run Commerce Committee took no action on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would force plants over 25 megawatts to cut nitrogen oxide emissions to a uniform nationwide floor or average emissions across units they own in a state [S3]. Utilities' interest in avoiding those control costs runs against the health interests of people downwind of their smokestacks.
Tighter emission limits on coal plants would reduce coal demand at the margin, since gas-fired and controlled units would gain an advantage [S3].
Retrofitting hundreds of large fossil units with nitrogen oxide controls would create demand for scrubber and combustion-control technology, with the public benefit arriving through cleaner air.
